extracted.intended_audience: NLP / ML researchers and practitioners working on LLM creative generation and evaluation (creative-writing + multi-agent systems)
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluation and generation of ~300-word science-fiction short stories produced by LLMs, including multi-agent generation protocols (LLM Review) and a unified evaluation pipeline combining LLM-as-a-judge, human annotation, and rule-based novelty/diversity metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: LLM-as-a-Judge: Scientific Concept Integration
rubrics_metrics.description: How well futuristic/scientific ideas are introduced, explained as needed, and woven into plot, setting, and character actions (not just name-dropped).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for clarity, relevance, and meaningful impact on the story’s events. Scored 0–5 (see global 0–5 rubric): 0 = potential plagiarism/very poor, 5 = highly creative and deeply integrated. The paper recommends evaluating each story three times with the judge and averaging scores to reduce variability.

rubrics_metrics.name: LLM-as-a-Judge: Speculative Logic
rubrics_metrics.description: The internal consistency and plausibility of the speculative elements given the story’s established rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess cause-and-effect coherence, logical constraints, and avoidance of convenient contradictions. Scored 0–5 per the shared Likert rubric; judge evaluations are aggregated and compared to human annotations for alignment.

rubrics_metrics.name: LLM-as-a-Judge: Character Depth
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinct, believable characters with motivations, agency, and emotional/psychological complexity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate growth, conflict, or meaningful choices that feel earned. Use the 0–5 scale; human annotators use same rubric to compute consensus scores for alignment analyses (ICC, Pearson r, Bland-Altman).

rubrics_metrics.name: LLM-as-a-Judge: Immersive World-Building
rubrics_metrics.description: A vivid, coherent story world with concrete details (culture, environment, technology, institutions) that support immersion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: World details should serve the narrative rather than overwhelm it. Judge and human scores averaged; judge is gpt-4o in experiments but the evaluation prompt template (system+user) defines the five-aspect scoring.

rubrics_metrics.name: LLM-as-a-Judge: Ethical and Philosophical Themes
rubrics_metrics.description: Presence and depth of ethical, societal, or philosophical questions typical of strong science fiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess nuance, originality, and integration into narrative stakes (not purely didactic). Scored 0–5 and compared against human annotator consensus to validate LLM-as-a-judge alignment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scoring scale (0–5) for all judge/human dimensions
rubrics_metrics.description: Shared Likert rubric used across the five LLM-as-a-judge dimensions and human annotation: 0–5 where 0 indicates potential plagiarism/very poor and 5 indicates exceptional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed scale: 0 = strong indicators of plagiarism or extremely low-quality/derivative writing; 1 = very weak; 2 = weak-to-fair; 3 = competent; 4 = strong; 5 = exceptional. Guidelines to annotators: use full scale, rate story as written, do not proofread grammar, provide independent judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule-based metric: Absolute Diversity (token-level surprisal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Intrinsic diversity measured as average token-level surprisal Savg = −(1/L) * sum_j log p(x_j | x_<j) where p(·) is the writer model's next-token probabilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surprisal focuses on information content of the tokens actually generated (normalized by length). Note: surprisal is model-distribution dependent and not comparable across different writer models; interpret alongside judge scores since high surprisal can reflect randomness rather than quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule-based metric: Lexical Divergence (KL divergence relative to SFGram)
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure lexical novelty using unigram KL divergence DKL(p∥q) where q(x) is unigram distribution from the SFGram reference corpus and p(x) is unigram distribution of generated text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply additive smoothing to avoid zero probabilities. Larger DKL indicates greater lexical deviation from traditional science fiction and serves as a proxy for lexical novelty; interpret together with judge scores to distinguish meaningful novelty from noise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule-based metric: Semantic Nearest-Neighbor Novelty (1 − max cosine similarity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Semantic novelty measured by embedding generated sentences and SFGram chunks, computing cosine similarity to each reference chunk and reporting 1 − max_cosine_similarity per generated sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Embeddings use all-mpnet-base-v2; SFGram is chunked (~250 words) due to encoder limits. Nearest-neighbor overlap captures local semantic overlap; higher 1 − max_cosine indicates higher novelty. Use in combination with other metrics since nearest-neighbor may miss distributional spread.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule-based metric: Embedding Volume Gain (∆vol = log det(Σ_ref∪story) − log det(Σ_ref))
rubrics_metrics.description: Measures how much adding the story expands embedding-space coverage of the reference corpus using log-determinant of covariance (generalized variance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Larger ∆vol indicates broader semantic spread beyond the reference corpus. Compute log det(Σ + ϵI) for numerical stability. Interpret alongside nearest-neighbor and lexical metrics: increased volume may indicate improved semantic coverage or merely randomness.

rubrics_metrics.name: SciFi-100 dataset: Ten creative-writing prompt aspects (dataset generation)
rubrics_metrics.description: SciFi-100 prompts were generated to evenly cover ten central aspects of creative writing (used to create 100 prompts total, 10 per aspect).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper lists example aspects/prompts used as dataset facets (see Table 6) and describes the data curation process: query LLMs to generate 20 prompts per aspect, then manually select/revise 10 per aspect to ensure diversity and thematic relevance. SciFi-100 is designed specifically to evaluate LLM short sci‑fi generation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aspect: Strong Voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Prompt aspect emphasizing a distinct narrative voice (e.g., perspective of a character with a specific tone like suspicion/curiosity/rebellious glee).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in prompt design to probe voice strength and stylistic distinctiveness in generated stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aspect: Imagery and Sensory Details
rubrics_metrics.description: Prompt aspect focusing on sensory-rich depiction (e.g., awe and danger observing a neutron star).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to elicit vivid descriptive language and perceptual detail from models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aspect: Conflict and Tension
rubrics_metrics.description: Prompt aspect that foregrounds an interpersonal or situational conflict to drive plot and stakes (e.g., persuading a skeptical alien committee).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designed to assess ability to create dramatic tension and persuasive narrative arcs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aspect: Character Development
rubrics_metrics.description: Prompt aspect that demands a character arc or overcoming of inner obstacles (e.g., researcher overcoming fear).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Probes generation of believable growth, motivations, and earned change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aspect: Emotional Impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Prompt aspect asking generation to evoke strong emotional response (e.g., discovery of life after decades of searching).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to evaluate affective resonance and pathos in short stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aspect: Show, Don't Tell
rubrics_metrics.description: Prompt aspect encouraging concrete behavior/sensory detail rather than exposition (e.g., late nights, notebook scribbles to show curiosity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tests ability to convey traits and motivations via scenes and actions rather than summary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aspect: Unique Plot or Theme
rubrics_metrics.description: Prompt aspect soliciting unusual or provocative plot premises and themes (e.g., live-streamed alien dissections with public reaction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assesses topical originality and thematic boldness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aspect: Pacing
rubrics_metrics.description: Prompt aspect focused on temporal structure and rhythm of events (e.g., build-up to a presentation then introspection).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Probes control of narrative time and momentum appropriate for ~300-word stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aspect: Symbolism and Metaphor
rubrics_metrics.description: Prompt aspect encouraging symbolic imagery used to represent thematic concerns (e.g., sealed lab door as secrecy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluates figurative language and deeper associative meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aspect: Effective Dialogue
rubrics_metrics.description: Prompt aspect requiring dialogue that reveals character and advances ethical or thematic conflict (e.g., scientists debating weaponization).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to test naturalistic, purposeful dialogue that serves narrative goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Production constraint: Target length ≈ 300 words
rubrics_metrics.description: Task definition specifies that generated short stories should be approximately 300 words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All frameworks (single-agent and multi-agent) use this target length to standardize evaluation and reduce variability due to length differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formatting constraint: story-only outputs (no commentary)
rubrics_metrics.description: All frameworks enforce the same formatting constraints: story text only, with no extraneous commentary or metadata.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reduces evaluation noise from off-format generations and ensures judge/annotation focus on story content alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multi-agent role-play constraints: persistent personas and N=3
rubrics_metrics.description: For multi-agent frameworks, agents are assigned persistent personas (e.g., Humanistic, Futuristic, Ecological) that remain fixed; default number of writer agents is N = 3.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personas are restated in prompts to encourage consistent viewpoints and reduce homogenization; experiments found N=3 yields best overall performance before feedback dilution occurs with more agents.

rubrics_metrics.name: LLM Review protocol (Blind Peer Review) — Compose Phase
rubrics_metrics.description: Each agent independently writes an initial story draft conditioned only on the prompt and its persona.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agents do not see peers' drafts during initial composition; this preserves independent creative trajectories.

rubrics_metrics.name: LLM Review protocol (Blind Peer Review) — Review Phase
rubrics_metrics.description: Each agent reviews peers’ initial drafts and provides targeted feedback on aspects like originality, world-building opportunities, speculative consistency, stronger imagery, character depth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Feedback is concrete and focused. Agents act as reviewers for peers (decentralized critique) to provide actionable revision cues without centralized steering.

rubrics_metrics.name: LLM Review protocol (Blind Peer Review) — Revision / Originality constraint
rubrics_metrics.description: Agents revise their own draft using (a) their initial draft and (b) the received feedback, but they do not see peers’ revised drafts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This information asymmetry (never exposing peers' revisions) is designed to reduce homogenization and preserve divergent trajectories while still benefiting from external critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation procedure: use LLM-as-a-judge + human annotation + rule-based metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Unified evaluation framework combines (i) LLM-as-a-judge scoring on five aspects (0–5), (ii) human annotation using the same five aspects and rubric, and (iii) rule-based novelty/diversity metrics (surprisal, KL, semantic measures).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: LLM-as-a-judge scores are averaged across three judge runs per story; human scores averaged across annotators (nine students in experiments). Rule-based metrics complement quality-aware judge scores because they capture divergence/novelty relative to SFGram.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation guidance: jointly interpret novelty metrics with quality scores
rubrics_metrics.description: Rule-based novelty metrics primarily capture divergence and not necessarily quality; large deviations may reflect randomness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Therefore, novelty/diversity metrics should be interpreted alongside LLM-as-a-judge (or human) quality scores to determine if novelty is meaningful creativity or low-quality noise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommended decoding hyperparameters and trade-offs
rubrics_metrics.description: Default decoding choices used in experiments: top_p ≈ 0.9 and temperature ≈ 0.9 (stochastic sampling).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ablations: increasing top_p from 0.7→1.0 improved Scientific Concept Integration and World-Building but could hurt Speculative Logic/Ethics at high entropy; increasing temperature boosts Concepts/World-Building but can degrade Logic and Ethics. Choose moderate values to balance creativity and coherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommended iterative design: rounds and number of agents
rubrics_metrics.description: Multi-agent frameworks in experiments run for R = 3 rounds; ablations show most dimensions peak at three rounds; using three agents yields best overall performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: More rounds or more agents can lead to selective improvements or uniform degradation due to feedback dilution; default R=3 and N=3 balance performance and efficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human evaluation protocol and annotator guidelines
rubrics_metrics.description: Human annotators rate each story on five 0–5 dimensions; instructions emphasize independent judgment, using full scale, rating story as written, and not proofreading grammar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recruitment criteria: age 18+, proficient English reading comprehension. Results reported in aggregate; human consensus scores are averaged across annotators for alignment analyses (ICC, Pearson r, Bland-Altman).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical & limitations guidance for evaluation and use
rubrics_metrics.description: Warnings that generated content may reflect biases, automated critique could reinforce shared assumptions, and LLM Review increases inference cost (~9× single-agent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Framework intended for research use with human oversight; novelty metrics limited by fixed reference corpus and may not by themselves guarantee meaningful creativity. Consider professional-writer evaluation for broader validation.
